title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
hook: the power goes out on a night with no moon. the hymn's third verse begins in that kind of dark

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's second verse: no death, no deathlessness, no night or day, and That One, breathing without wind. Did a big question stay open while the breath went on? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

The power goes out on a night with no moon. You shut your eyes, then open them, and you can't tell the difference. The dark behind your eyelids and the dark of the room have become one dark. Your hand is somewhere in front of your face, but you couldn't prove it. Nothing has an edge. Nothing stands out from anything else. The Nasadiya Sukta's third verse begins in that kind of dark, and then pushes it further than any power cut could. Today: what the hymn says was there at the start, and the one thing that changed it.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `EYES OPEN, EYES SHUT: THE SAME.` → `NOTHING HAS AN EDGE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit the verse opens tama asit tamasa gulham agre. Darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning. Not darkness covering something. Darkness covering darkness. Nothing to see, and nothing to see it with. The verse goes on, in paraphrase: all this was water, with no mark on it, nothing told apart from anything else. That's the hymn's picture of the start. Not an empty space with sharp edges, but a sameness so complete that nothing could stand out. Then comes the turn. What was coming into being, the verse says, lay covered by emptiness, and that One was born by the power of tapas. Tapas is a word for heat. Later Hindu tradition also uses it for another kind of heat, the glow a person builds through vows, fasting and long sitting. Here, at the very start, the hymn uses it for the warmth by which the One came to be. Notice what the verse leaves out. It doesn't say who made the heat. It doesn't name a god striking a spark. So far the hymn has asked questions it doesn't answer, and it doesn't break that honesty now. It only gives an order. First, sameness, dark on dark. Then, warmth. Then, one thing that could be told apart from the rest. That order isn't only cosmic. A frozen pond is one flat gray sheet until warmth reaches it; then the ice gives, and the water starts to move. The hymn is talking about the beginning of everything, not about kitchens, but the shape is one a person can recognize: before anything has a name, something warms.
screen: `DARKNESS HIDDEN BY DARKNESS.` · `WATER WITH NO MARK ON IT.` · `THE ONE, BORN BY THE POWER OF HEAT.` · `SAMENESS, THEN WARMTH, THEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the dark be dark for a while. If you can, close your eyes, or lower your gaze. Let the dark behind your eyelids be as plain as it is. Don't try to make pictures in it. Then find one warm thing in the body: the breath at the nostrils, the hands resting together, the middle of the chest. Rest your attention on that warmth, and let the rest stay dark around it. When a thought pulls you off, come back to the warm place. If you pray, you can let that warmth be an offering. The bell holds the time.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its third verse, darkness hidden by darkness, until the One was born by the power of heat. Today's word.

Your line: the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation, who really knows? Today, when something feels stuck and the same, a task, a conversation, a quiet room, notice what warms it into moving. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: The Nasadiya Sukta is part of the Rig Veda, and like other Vedic hymns it is kept in traditional recitation, learned by memory from a teacher.

fork.setup: you're the poet. everything is dark and the same. what brings the first one thing into being?
fork.reveal: the third verse says the One was born by the power of tapas, heat. it doesn't say where the heat came from.

original.note: Sanskrit: heat. In Rig Veda 10.129.3 the One is born by its power; later texts also use it for the heat of discipline.

trapdoor: what you thought: a creation hymn starts with a maker doing something.
what it means: this verse starts with sameness, darkness hidden by darkness, and the One born by the power of heat.
what a scholar hears: tapasas tan mahinajayataikam, 'by the greatness of tapas that One was born,' with tapas the same word later used for the heat of ascetic discipline.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.129.3 (all this was undistinguished water; what was coming to be was covered by the void; that One was born by the power of tapas)

notes: Days 1250 (verse 1) and 1251 (verse 2) were checked after writing; this day takes verse 3, and 1253–1255 take verses 4, 5 and 6–7. The review picks up 1251.
Sanskrit of 10.129.3a (tama āsīt tamasā gūḷham agre) and 3d (tapasas tan mahinājāyataikam) given from memory in simplified transliteration; confirm.
Paraphrase of 3b–c: 'all this was water with no mark on it' (apraketaṃ salilam), 'what was coming into being lay covered by emptiness' (tucchyenābhv apihitam). Confirm.
Claim that later Hindu texts use tapas for the heat of vows, fasting and austerity: standard, but confirm the wording. No etymology is claimed.
The kitchen and blank-page images are offered as the writer's analogy, explicitly not as the hymn's meaning.

Editor: fixed an ordering error (the hymn's 'who could know' question comes in verse 6, not before verse 3); softened 'later Hindu texts' to 'later tradition'; replaced the stove and blank-page images, which repeated 1244's lit stove and 1254's blank sheet, with a frozen pond; carry reworded to match.
